summary: Revises the way IP and ARP are carried on HIPPI, a high-speed interconnect, building on an ANSI standard for encapsulating IEEE 802.2 LLC PDUs. It is intended to replace an earlier RFC on the Standards Track.

eli5.summary: This describes how to carry internet packets over a very fast computer cable.

subtitle: How IP datagrams are wrapped and sent across HIPPI, a very fast parallel link, when HIPPI switches are used as a local area network.

tldr.problem: The ANSI HIPPI standards describe the channel, the framing, the encapsulation of IEEE 802.2 LLC and the switch, but leave open how to use a HIPPI switch as an IP local area network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2067 fixes one packet layout (HIPPI-FP, HIPPI-LE, 802.2 LLC/SNAP, then the IP datagram), the I-field contents, a 65280-byte MTU and connection rules such as a 68-burst limit per connection.
tldr.outcome: It revises RFC 1374, drops the ARP part into a separate document and removes some packet format options. It is listed as a Draft Standard.

facts.label: Data rate
facts.value: Nearly 800 Mbit/s, with a 1600 Mbit/s option

today: RFC 2067 is listed as a Draft Standard, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. Its header says it replaces RFC 1374 on the Standards Track, with the ARP description moved to a separate Informational memo.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The ANSI High-Performance Parallel Interface (HIPPI) is a simplex data channel. Used in pairs, it can send and receive at nearly 800 megabits per second at the same time, and there is a 1600 megabit/second option. Four ANSI documents cover the physical layer (HIPPI-PH), framing (HIPPI-FP), encapsulation of IEEE 802.2 LLC (HIPPI-LE) and the behavior of a physical layer switch (HIPPI-SC).

The working group stopped short of describing HIPPI switches as local area networks. This memo picks up there. Its guiding principle is that, apart from length and hardware header, an Internet datagram sent on HIPPI should be identical to the same datagram on a conventional network, and any datagram valid on a conventional 802 network should be valid on HIPPI.
sections.eli5: HIPPI is a very fast two-way cable. This memo explains how to send ordinary internet packets over it so they look the same as on any other network.

sections.title: Scope and Changes from RFC 1374
sections.content:
The memo covers the HIPPI interface between a host and a crosspoint switch that follows HIPPI-SC. Hosts that comply are believed to interoperate on a network made of a single HIPPI-SC switch, or on a point-to-point HIPPI connection with no switch. Inside scope are the packet format and headers, the I-field contents and the rules for using connections. Address resolution (ARP), network configuration and management, host internal optimizations and the interface to an outboard protocol processor are outside it.

This document revises RFC 1374, which had been a Proposed Standard since November 1992. The ARP description was moved to a separate Informational memo for lack of implementation experience. Three options RFC 1374 allowed are now forbidden: an optional short burst first, D1 fill bytes, and a nonzero D2 offset. The memo says no RFC 1374 implementation used them, so interoperability problems are not expected. The word SHALL marks mandatory points.
sections.eli5: This memo is a cleaned-up second edition. It drops a few rarely used choices so everyone builds the packets the same way.

sections.title: The HIPPI Packet Format
sections.content:
An IP packet on HIPPI is built in layers. The HIPPI-FP header (8 bytes) comes first, then the HIPPI-LE header (24 bytes) in the D1 area. The D2 area carries one IEEE 802.2 Type 1 LLC Unnumbered Information PDU: an 8-byte LLC/SNAP header followed by the IP datagram. Fill of 0 to 7 bytes makes the whole packet a multiple of eight bytes. The D1_Area_Size is 3 (64-bit words), and D2_Size must not exceed 65,288.

The LLC header uses SSAP 170 and DSAP 170 ('AA'h) with control value 3. The SNAP organization code is zero and the EtherType is set from Assigned Numbers: IP is 2048 ('0800'h), ARP is 2054 ('0806'h) and RARP is 32,821 ('8035'h). Any short burst must be the last burst of the packet.

Message_Type in the HIPPI-LE header says what the PDU is. Destination and source switch addresses are 24-bit fields, right justified when shorter, and each has a 4-bit address type: 0 unspecified, 1 HIPPI-SC source route (24 bits), 2 HIPPI-SC address (12 bits). The 48-bit IEEE addresses hold the Universal LAN MAC address if known, otherwise zero.
sections.eli5: The packet is a set of nested envelopes: a HIPPI envelope, a second one saying who is who, a label that says it holds IP, and then the real message inside.

sections.title: Addresses and the I-Field
sections.content:
Each node on a HIPPI-SC LAN should get a 48-bit Universal LAN Address (ULA). Using ULAs is optional but encouraged. HIPPI-SC switches do not use them, but they can help with switch address resolution, telling apart several logical entities in one node, and gateways that swap the HIPPI header for another LAN's MAC header.

The I-field is the 32 bits a Source sends when it requests a connection. In this memo the Locally Administered bit is zero and the Double wide bit is set only when the Source wants a 64 bit connection. Path Selection is 00 (source route mode, a 24-bit route), 01 or 11 (logical address mode with 12-bit addresses), at the Source's option. With 11 the switch may choose among routes, and 01 forces the same route for the same pair. In logical address mode the Destination Address holds the destination's Switch Address.

Camp-on may be 1 or 0, but a Source must not make consecutive requests without it to the same Destination while they are being rejected, because that would defeat the switch's fair share arbitration.
sections.eli5: Every computer has a name tag. To start a conversation, the sender first sends a short note to the switch saying which tag it wants to reach, a bit like dialing a phone number.

sections.title: Rules for Connections and Camp-on
sections.content:
The connection rules give Sources frequent, fair access to a Destination that many Sources want. A Source may hold a connection for as long as it takes to send 68 HIPPI bursts, over all packets in that connection. One packet per connection is acceptable. The limit is not absolute, but a Source sending 64K packets must check at the end of each packet so it does not send a second one (two would be 130 bursts).

Sources must not assert REQUEST until a packet is ready, must send bursts as fast as READYs allow, and must drop REQUEST when nothing more is ready. Destinations must reject all connections if they cannot receive packets, accept a connection immediately when buffers are available, and, once initialized, reject only for bad I-field parity or invalid I-field contents. They must not abort a connection merely because too many bursts arrived, and must treat aborted connection sequences as normal.

Camp-on asks the switch to wait until a busy Destination is free. Without it, a rejection could come from the Destination or the switch, with no reason given, so a Source should not treat it as an error. Switching time matters most for throughput: ten microseconds permits nearly full HIPPI throughput with full-sized packets, and at 60 microseconds throughput drops by about 10%.
sections.eli5: It is like a shared water fountain with a queue. Nobody may drink for too long, and if the fountain is busy you take a number and wait instead of pestering the person using it.

sections.title: MTU and Path MTU Discovery
sections.content:
HIPPI itself has no practical packet size limit, since the 32-bit D2_Size field allows about 4 gigabytes. A HIPPI-SC LAN still needs an MTU so Destinations can size buffers, and this memo sets it at 65280 bytes. That lets the IP packet fit in one 64K byte buffer with up to 256 bytes of overhead. The overhead is 40 bytes today (8 for HIPPI-FP, 24 for HIPPI-LE, 8 for LLC/SNAP), leaving 216 bytes for expansion.

HIPPI nodes can use the Path MTU Discovery method of RFC 1191 without change, and gateways between HIPPI-SC LANs and other networks should implement it.
sections.eli5: Everything has to fit in one big box of a fixed size. The box is almost 64K, with a little spare room in case the labels on it get bigger later.

sections.title: Channel Data Rate Discovery
sections.content:
HIPPI comes in 800 and 1600 megabit/second options. The faster one is 64 bits wide: Cable B carries 32 extra data bits and four parity bits next to Cable A. The W bit in the I-field asks for a 64-bit connection. A 64-bit Source can reach a 32-bit Destination by clearing W and not using Cable B. If W is set and the Destination has only Cable A, the switch rejects the request.

The same is true if the path goes through a link only 32 bits wide. The only reliable way to learn what a path supports is to try a 64-bit connection with Camp-on. If it is rejected, try 32 bits. If that works, assume the Destination or path is not double width and use 32-bit requests from then on. If that is also rejected, assume the Destination or path is down. Camp-on is needed on the 64-bit try because otherwise a reject could just mean the Destination was busy. The Double_Wide bit in the HIPPI-LE header gives the receiver a hint that a 64-bit attempt on the return path may be worthwhile.
sections.eli5: It is like trying a wide door first. If you cannot get through, you try the narrow one. If both are shut, the room is probably closed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that security issues are not discussed in the memo. There is no authentication, encryption or access control defined here beyond the Destination's option to reject connections when the I-field contents are invalid, for example when the Source is not permitted to send to it.

The text does add one warning about sharing a switch. Applications that hold connections too long on links shared with network traffic may cause loss of network packets or serious degradation of network service.
sections.eli5: The memo does not talk about keeping bad guys out. It only warns that if one user hogs a shared cable, everyone else's messages can get lost or slowed down.

fields.name: FC
fields.desc: Zero unless defined by local administration.

fields.name: Double_Wide
fields.desc: One if the Destination paired with the sending Source supports 64 bit operation.

fields.name: Message_Type
fields.desc: Identifies the type of HIPPI-LE PDU; 0 is a data PDU.

fields.name: Destination_Switch_Address
fields.desc: Switch Address of the Destination if known, otherwise zero.

fields.name: Source Address Type
fields.desc: Same codes, for the source address.

fields.name: Destination_IEEE_Address
fields.desc: 48 bit Universal LAN MAC address of the Destination if known, otherwise zero.

fields.name: LE_Locally_Administered
fields.desc: Zero unless defined by local administration.

fields.name: Source_IEEE_Address
fields.desc: 48 bit Universal LAN MAC address of the Source if known, otherwise zero.

items.label: Data PDU
items.desc: Carries data, such as an IP datagram.
